title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator–Predictor View of Attention and MLPs

paper.title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator–Predictor View of Attention and MLPs
paper.abstract:
Abstract How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize?
We develop an aggregator–predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers , in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs.
We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius.
We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation.
Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key–value representation for tokenwise patch prediction.
Our experiments support this view.
DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern.
In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance.
Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction.
Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-matching models are widely used for image generation ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) becoming a standard backbone ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Li and He, 2026 ) . Growing evidence connects their generalization to representations of images and rules for reusing them . Diffusion features encode semantic and geometric information ( Baranchuk et al., 2022 ; Tang et al., 2023 ) , and aligning them with pretrained representations improves training ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Models also generate combinations absent from the training data, as shown by analyses of synthetic hierarchical data ( Okawa et al., 2023 ; Favero et al., 2025 ) . How components of DiTs realize these capabilities remains unclear. Existing explanations connect diffusion-model generalization to geometry-adaptive harmonic or balanced representations ( Kadkhodaie et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and inductive biases toward spatial locality and translation equivariance ( Kamb and Ganguli, 2025 ; Niedoba et al., 2025 ) . These accounts leave open how DiT components divide the denoising computation. Rosu et al. (2025) show that attention can implement exact score-based denoising, but they consider whole-image tokens, leaving interactions among spatial patches unresolved. An et al. (2025) associate DiT generalization with attention mimicking CNN-like spatial locality, but attention can also select input-dependent, spatially non-contiguous context (Sec. 5.1 ). We ask: How do attention, MLPs, and adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) divide the work of representing image content and learning context-dependent rules for generalization? Understanding these component roles matters for intervention: domain adaptation, concept editing, and controlled generation require deciding which computations to modify and which to preserve. In language models, interpreting MLPs as key–value memories has motivated methods for editing stored associations ( Geva et al., 2021 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ) , with related analyses in multimodal transformers ( Pan et al., 2024a ; Basu et al., 2024a ) . A functional account of DiTs could similarly guide component-wise adaptation across domains and interventions that change image content while preserving desired spatial relationships. Related work is reviewed in Appendix A . We address this question by proposing an aggregator–predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers , supported by a statistical foundation and a set of architectural and empirical observations: (1) A statistical foundation for local denoising. We justify local denoiser, in which each patch is denoised using only a subset of context patches, by identifying its statistical target and establishing when it approximates the global Bayes denoiser. Specifically, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) image priors, the global denoiser can be approximated by a radius- r r local denoiser with error decaying exponentially in r r (Thm. 1 ). We further connect existing patchwise retrieval-based explanations of generalization to this target by showing that, with sufficiently informative aggregation, a patchwise linear denoiser exactly recovers the empirical local denoiser (Thm. 3 ). (2) An aggregator–predictor interpretation of DiT components. We decompose the local denoising into context aggregation followed by patch prediction (Def. 2 ). Under this view, the algebraic structure of AdaLN-modulated attention implements an input- and noise-dependent aggregation rule: QK parameterizes spatial compatibility weights, while VO transforms the corresponding features (Sec. 4.1 ). In turn, MLP admits a key–value memory interpretation and operates on the resulting contextualized token (Sec. 4.2 ). These algebraic correspondences are exact for the isolated branches considered in Sec. 4 ; in a multilayer residual stack, the proposed roles interact and need not remain functionally separable (Appendix D.5 ). This view extends existing fixed spatial-locality accounts by allowing the relevant context to depend on the image and noise level and to include spatially non-contiguous patches. It further suggests the possibility of replacing DiT MLPs with more interpretable memory-based components, as supported by our experiments (Sec. 5.2 ). (3) Empirical evidence consistent with the proposed component roles. Across real-image datasets, DiT sensitivity fields exhibit noise-dependent context broadening resembling the GMRF setting, while attention mass shows a related qualitative trend (Sec. 5.1 ). We further construct explicit shared-memory patch predictors that retain competitive denoising and generation performance in a controlled CelebA64 study (Sec. 5.2 ). Finally, cross-domain component transplantation reveals systematic component-compatibility patterns associated with source–target spatial similarity. These patterns are consistent with, but do not uniquely identify, the proposed roles in context aggregation and patch prediction (Sec. 5.3 ).

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments examine whether trained DiT denoisers exhibit locality patterns resembling those of the oracle GMRF denoiser (Sec. 5.1 ), and whether, as suggested by our aggregator–predictor framework, layerwise MLPs can be replaced with more interpretable, shared-memory patch predictors (Sec. 5.2 ). Finally, we use component transplantation to examine whether compatibility patterns among jointly adapted QK, VO, and MLP parameters are consistent with this framework (Sec. 5.3 ). Experimental details and additional results are in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5.1 Real-image denoising echoes GMRF locality
sections.text: Figure 3: Sensitivity-defined contexts broaden with noise, with attention mass showing a related trend. Gold/white contours enclose 50%/95% of normalized squared sensitivity or attention mass; ticks point inward and cyan dots mark target patches. Right: 95% radii averaged over target patches; Details in Appendix E.2 . An exact analysis as in Fig. 2 is unavailable for real images. Instead, we identify context sets using sensitivity weights , which quantify how the prediction of patch m m responds to perturbations of input patch l l , based on a trained DiT’s Jacobian, similar to Niedoba et al. (2025) . The population denoiser’s Jacobian measures posterior dependence between clean patches given the noisy patches ( Dytso et al., 2021 ) . Based on these weights, we define the q q -sensitivity radius as the smallest radius of a square centered on patch m m containing at least a fraction q q of the total weight. The sensitivity context set contains the fewest patches carrying at least that fraction. Denoising sensitivity exhibits GMRF-like broadening; attention shows a related trend. For the synthetic GMRF where the true Jacobian is available, Fig. 2 (c) shows that sensitivity spreads over broader contexts as noise increases. Denoising real images echoes this pattern: Fig. 3 shows concentrated sensitivity at low noise and broader, sometimes disconnected contexts at higher noise, together with increasing sensitivity radii. Notably, replacing sensitivity weights with attention mass yields analogous attention contexts and radii, which also generally broaden with noise. Together, these observations support the GMRF setting as a tractable reference model for denoising locality and the interpretation of attention as an input-adaptive context aggregator. Sensitivity and attention mass measure different quantities, so the comparison concerns a shared qualitative trend rather than identical context sets. Additional results appear in Appendix E.2 . Figure 4: Shared-memory patch predictors at comparable parameter budgets. Models are trained on CelebA64 for 400 epochs; see Appendix E.3 for details.

sections.heading: 5.2 Shared-memory predictors can replace MLPs in a controlled setting
sections.text: We replace DiT MLPs with LPLD, SCA, and SMLP on CelebA64. We compare similar parameter budgets using a common backbone architecture, with modest models and one training seed per configuration for unconditional 64 × 64 64\times 64 face generation. Figure 4 reports held-out velocity loss, denoising error, and FID at epoch 400. Three patterns appear; first, the patch-shared SCA and SMLP banks outperform the position-specific LPLD bank at comparable parameter budgets, showing that competitive prediction need not assign separate memory for every patch position. Second, SMLP improves on SCA, supporting unnormalized GELU retrieval as an effective alternative to softmax. Third, SMLP with H = 8 H=8 achieves competitive denoising and lower FID than the ordinary MLP, despite sharing its base memory across layers. Multiple predictor heads generally improve performance, suggesting that multiple projections of the shared bank can be useful. Together, these results demonstrate that an explicit, layer-shared memory bank can support competitive patch prediction in this controlled setting. We note that these results by themselves do not establish that layerwise MLP parameters generally encode a single shared memory or that this design transfers unchanged to larger conditional DiTs. Training details and limitations are in Appendix E.3 . Figure 5: QK, VO, and MLP component transplants. (a) Source-QK compatibility is higher across spatially similar datasets. (b) VO reversion costs more as joint non-additivity increases. (c) Natural-image source QK retains partial agreement on face targets. See Appendix E.4.2 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Component transplants support the aggregator–predictor view
sections.text: Transplanting jointly adapted components probes compatibility and coadaptation. To examine compatibility patterns in relation to the proposed component roles, we fine-tune a pretrained source model on a target dataset. We then transplant combinations of the adapted components into the source checkpoint. When the datasets have similar spatial structure, our framework suggests that source QK may remain compatible with adapted VO and MLP parameters. Larger spatial shifts may be associated with stronger coadaptation. We study twelve transfer directions between face and natural-image datasets. For clarity, we jointly fine-tune only QK, VO, and MLP, leaving AdaLN and all other parameters fixed, assuming that the learned time conditioning transfers across domains. Each of the eight resulting hybrids is labeled by QK/VO/MLP bits: 0 for source weights and 1 for jointly adapted weights. These transplants probe the compatibility and coadaptation of parameters learned jointly; they do not measure the performance obtainable by training QK-, VO-, or MLP-only models. Separately, under the same target-domain update budget, QK-only and QK+VO-only fine-tuning generally fall further behind joint adaptation on larger domain shifts (Appendix E.4.5 ). Following work on patch self-similarity and spatial normalization ( Tumanyan et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) , we measure spatial distance between datasets using MMD 2 of patch self-similarity descriptors. We compare each hybrid’s outputs with the fully adapted model’s using matched initial noise. We measure this agreement using DINOv2 global features for endpoint agreement (EA) and patch self-similarity patterns for spatial agreement (SA). Both scores assign 0 to the source and 1 to the fully adapted model. Full protocols and results are in Appendix E.4 . QK compatibility is higher for spatially similar datasets, while VO reversion penalties track component coadaptation. With source QK retained (011), CelebA → \to AAHQ/FFHQ/AFHQ produces recognizable faces. In contrast, among the tested CelebA → \to STL-10 hybrids, coherent target-like structure emerges primarily only when all jointly adapted components are present (111; Figs. 1 and 13 ). Consistent with this pattern, the QK reversion penalty tends to increase with spatial distance (Fig. 5 (a)), which also accompanies stronger component coadaptation (Appendix E.4.3 ). Additionally, restoring source VO (101) yields fragmented textures in the natural-image-to-face transfers (Figs. 14 and 15 ). Its reversion penalty increases with joint non-additivity—the gain from joint adaptation beyond the sum of isolated component changes (Fig. 5 (b)). Source QK from broader natural-image domains retains partial compatibility on face targets. With source QK retained (011), STL-10 hybrids recover human and animal face structure, including a blurred face for STL-10 → \to CelebA, while joint adaptation produces clearer results (Fig. 14 ). This contrasts with the poorly formed scene in the reverse CelebA → \to STL-10 direction (Fig. 1 ); additional examples in Appendix E.4.4 . Figure 5 (c) supports this asymmetry: source QK from STL-10 retains greater endpoint agreement on CelebA than in the reverse direction, while QK from natural-image domains retains partial agreement on face targets at levels comparable to CelebA QK.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: We presented an aggregator–predictor view of diffusion transformers as input-adaptive local denoisers. Our theory justifies local denoising under GMRF priors and connects patchwise linear denoisers to the empirical local denoising target. Within this framework, QK determines spatial context weights, VO transports features, and MLPs perform contextualized patch prediction. Experiments provide complementary evidence through noise-dependent denoising contexts, competitive shared-memory predictors, and cross-domain component compatibility patterns. Together, these findings offer a statistical and architectural perspective on DiT denoising and motivate further work on interpretable predictors and targeted model adaptation. Our experiments focus on modest-sized, unconditional DiTs operating on 64 × 64 64\times 64 images across a limited collection of face and natural-image datasets. In particular, the shared-memory predictor comparison uses CelebA64 with one training seed per configuration, leaving its robustness across datasets, model scales, and training seeds unresolved. The transfer study examines twelve directions while keeping AdaLN and global parameters fixed; its component transplants probe compatibility among jointly adapted weights and do not uniquely identify the proposed functional roles. Testing these patterns in larger conditional models, at higher resolutions, and under broader adaptation protocols is an important next step.

sections.heading: Representations and compositional reuse.
sections.text: Diffusion models learn internal features useful for semantic segmentation and discriminative probing ( Baranchuk et al., 2022 ; Xiang et al., 2023 ) , and semantic and geometric correspondence can emerge without correspondence supervision ( Tang et al., 2023 ) . Chen et al. (2025) connect this ability to classical denoising autoencoders by simplifying diffusion models and studying which components support self-supervised representation learning. Han et al. (2025a) provide theoretical and empirical evidence that denoising encourages representations covering multiple data features, including features that classifiers may neglect. REPA connects representation quality to generative training by aligning hidden states with pretrained visual features in diffusion and flow-based transformers ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Singh et al. (2026) further identify the spatial structure of the alignment target as a strong predictor of generation performance. Compositional generation provides evidence of reuse: Okawa et al. (2023) demonstrate unseen combinations in a synthetic task, and Favero et al. (2025) analyze the learning of composition rules in a hierarchical grammar, where longer-range dependencies require more data. The extent of this ability depends on the task; Han et al. (2025b) find that diffusion models can learn coarse relationships while failing finer dependencies, including reflection and lighting consistency. These findings motivate the introduction’s representation-and-reuse framing. In our denoising account, a reuse rule has a specific meaning: it determines which context patches supply evidence for predicting a clean patch from a new noisy image.

sections.heading: Memorization and generalization.
sections.text: Under a finite empirical prior, the squared-error denoising objective is minimized by a weighted average of training images, with weights determined by whole-image comparisons as in ( 2 ). With the corresponding terminal initialization, exact reverse dynamics recover the empirical distribution ( Pidstrigach, 2022 ; Yoon et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Kamb and Ganguli, 2025 ) . Several explanations address why learned denoisers nevertheless generalize. Training dynamics can favor generalizing solutions before memorization, with larger datasets delaying memorization ( Bonnaire et al., 2025 ) ; large learning rates can also steer training away from the memorizing solution ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . Other accounts characterize the learned estimator: Kadkhodaie et al. (2024) connect generalization to geometry-adaptive harmonic representations, while Zhang et al. (2026) prove a distinction between sample storage and balanced representations of local statistics for a two-layer ReLU denoising autoencoder, and investigate analogous structure in larger models. Our framework concerns how DiT components implement denoising computations compatible with such statistical structure.

sections.heading: Local denoising and its statistical target.
sections.text: Local empirical denoisers explain novel generation through patch recombination. Niedoba et al. (2025) use cropped neighborhoods to approximate trained denoisers; Kamb and Ganguli (2025) derive estimators from locality and translation equivariance; and Lukoianov et al. (2025) choose context from the sensitivity of the optimal linear denoiser, emphasizing the role of data statistics. These constructions motivate the patchwise linear denoiser (PLD) in Section 2 . In ( 3 ), a softmax comparison through S m , t S_{m,t} determines how stored training patches x m ( i ) x_{m}^{(i)} contribute to a prediction. Setting S m , t = I S_{m,t}=I and Γ m , t = σ t − 2 ​ I \Gamma_{m,t}=\sigma_{t}^{-2}I recovers whole-image retrieval; local contexts allow the weights to differ across patches and hence permit recombination. Our statistical contribution identifies a population target for this construction. Theorem 1 bounds the discrepancy between population local and global denoisers under a GMRF prior. Theorem 3 identifies when sufficient aggregation lets a PLD recover the empirical local conditional mean exactly; this identity alone is not a finite-sample bound on population risk. Together, the results motivate learning both the context aggregator and the patch predictor. The stored patches and context comparisons in the PLD provide an explicit example of content and reuse; Section 4 develops their learned counterparts in a DiT.

sections.heading: Architectural accounts of denoising.
sections.text: Mei (2025) show how U-Net encoder–decoder paths and skip connections can implement belief-propagation denoising in hierarchical graphical models, providing a direct precedent for interpreting architecture through a statistical denoising algorithm. For transformers, Rosu et al. (2025) show that attention can implement exact score-based denoising; their image experiments use whole-image tokens, although an anisotropic extension permits patchwise pixel updates. An et al. (2025) associate DiT generalization with local attention in early layers and show benefits from restricting attention windows with limited training data. Gan et al. (2025) link concentrated large feature activations to AdaLN and use channel modulation to improve DiT features for correspondence. These works explain architectural or conditioning mechanisms relevant to denoising and representation learning. Our account connects attention, MLPs, and AdaLN through context aggregation followed by patch prediction, allowing context to vary with the input and noise level, including the non-contiguous patterns in Section 5.1 .

sections.heading: MLPs as learned memory.
sections.text: Language-model MLPs have been interpreted as key–value memories that store and retrieve learned associations ( Petroni et al., 2019 ; Geva et al., 2021 ; Geva et al., 2022 ) ; Sukhbaatar et al. (2019) express them as attention over persistent memory vectors. This interpretation has motivated locating and editing facts through MLP weights ( Dai et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ) , with related analyses and interventions in multimodal models ( Schwettmann et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024a ; Basu et al., 2024a ; Pan et al., 2024b ) . At the level of the generative process, Hoover et al. (2023) survey connections between diffusion dynamics and retrieval in energy-based associative memories. Our DiT account assigns a memory role specifically to the MLP’s patch prediction from aggregated context (Section 4.2 ). Replacing layerwise MLPs with explicit memory shared across layers tests this interpretation at the level of the predictor component (Section 5.2 ). The representation may be distributed across learned memory entries; the interpretation does not require individual entries to correspond to named concepts.

sections.heading: Localization, editing, and component interventions.
sections.text: Several analyses of text-to-image diffusion localize visual attributes in text-encoder self-attention or U-Net cross-attention ( Basu et al., 2024c ; Basu et al., 2024b ) , including neurons associated with concepts or memorized training images ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Hintersdorf et al., 2024 ) . For DiTs, Zarei et al. (2025) identify blocks associated with specific concepts and use localized updates for personalization and unlearning. Their component ablations also intervene on self-attention, normalization, and MLP outputs, with cross-attention giving the strongest localization signal in the tested PixArt setting. Thus, component intervention already has direct precedents in DiTs. Related editing methods illustrate the practical value of these distinctions. Custom Diffusion adapts selected parameters for concept customization ( Kumari et al., 2023 ) ; Plug-and-Play Diffusion Features injects spatial features and self-attention to preserve layout during translation ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) ; and Shin et al. (2025) analyze text–image attention blocks to design editing interventions for multimodal DiTs. Turri et al. (2026) further show that transferring high-magnitude hidden-state channels between prompt-conditioned trajectories can steer image semantics in DiT and related flow-based models. These activation interventions complement our parameter transplants, which ask which QK, VO, and MLP computations remain compatible across image domains, guided by the aggregator–predictor account (Section 5.3 ). The transplants probe jointly adapted components with AdaLN fixed, so their outcomes measure reuse and coadaptation under that intervention protocol (Appendix E.4 ).

sections.heading: Gaussian and Markov image priors.
sections.text: The GMRF prior in Theorem 1 combines joint Gaussian statistics with conditional independence between non-neighboring patches given their graph neighbors. Markov image models developed from spatial statistics ( Besag, 1974 ) into methods for restoration, texture modeling, and segmentation ( Geman and Geman, 1984 ; Li, 2009 ) , with higher-order models extending interactions to larger neighborhoods and patches ( Roth and Black, 2005 ; Weiss and Freeman, 2007 ; Chen et al., 2014 ) . Gaussian MRFs ( Rue and Held, 2005 ) have been used for texture modeling ( Chellappa and Chatterjee, 1985 ) , Bayesian restoration ( Shouno, 2015 ; Yasuda et al., 2018 ; Monma et al., 2022 ) , and learned conditional denoising ( Tappen et al., 2007 ) . The Gaussian optimal denoiser is the Wiener filter ( Wiener, 1949 ; Andrews and Hunt, 1977 ) ; its tractability also supports exact analyses of diffusion sampling ( Pierret and Galerne, 2025 ) and approximations to learned scores at high noise ( Wang and Vastola, 2024 ) . We use this tractable prior with patches as variables on an arbitrary graph to establish a locality guarantee, and examine the corresponding qualitative patterns on real images separately.

sections.heading: D.5 From a single layer to a residual stack
sections.text: The construction in Sec. 4 isolates aggregation and prediction in a single layer without residual connections. In this section, we explain its extension to a residual stack , a multilayer architecture with residual connections. Let h ℓ h_{\ell} denote the hidden token sequence entering layer ℓ \ell at diffusion time t t . We absorb normalization, AdaLN, and output gates into the attention branch 𝒮 ℓ , t attn \mathcal{S}_{\ell,t}^{\mathrm{attn}} and the tokenwise predictor g ℓ , t g_{\ell,t} (an MLP in DiT). The two residual additions give s ℓ \displaystyle s_{\ell} = h ℓ + 𝒮 ℓ , t attn ​ ( h ℓ ) , \displaystyle=h_{\ell}+\mathcal{S}_{\ell,t}^{\mathrm{attn}}(h_{\ell}), h ℓ + 1 \displaystyle h_{\ell+1} = s ℓ + g ℓ , t ​ ( s ℓ ) = h ℓ + 𝒮 ℓ , t attn ​ ( h ℓ ) + g ℓ , t ​ ( h ℓ + 𝒮 ℓ , t attn ​ ( h ℓ ) ) ⏟ F ℓ , t ​ ( h ℓ ) . \displaystyle=s_{\ell}+g_{\ell,t}(s_{\ell})=h_{\ell}+\underbrace{\mathcal{S}_{\ell,t}^{\mathrm{attn}}(h_{\ell})+g_{\ell,t}\!\left(h_{\ell}+\mathcal{S}_{\ell,t}^{\mathrm{attn}}(h_{\ell})\right)}_{F_{\ell,t}(h_{\ell})}. (28) The aggregator interpretation also applies to s ℓ s_{\ell} : it combines the token’s existing state with attention-selected context, so the identity path retains a contribution from the token itself. The predictor then maps this contextualized state to a residual feature update. We emphasize that ( 28 ) motivates interpreting the residual stack as iterative denoising in feature space : successive aggregation and prediction updates refine the internal residual stream from which the final clean-image estimate is read out. This view is consistent with interpretations of residual networks as unrolled iterative estimation and feature refinement ( Greff et al., 2017 ; Jastrzebski et al., 2018 ) . This interpretation also motivates consulting a shared memory across depth, providing a reusable bank of learned representations at each refinement step. However, the clean factorization in a single layer does not necessarily extend to a residual stack. Patch projection and positional embedding are applied once at network entry; later layers operate on already contextualized tokens. Although the shared-channel-operator decomposition of attention still holds layerwise, a token can depend on many original patches, and VO or predictor updates can alter later QK routing. The division of labor between QK and VO is therefore less clear-cut than in a single layer. Similarly, the MLP in one layer can affect attention in subsequent layers, and attention can in turn affect subsequent MLP updates.

sections.text: We conduct experiments to illustrate the concept of local context and examine the prediction of Cor. 2 : within a specified noise interval, the radius certifying an upper bound on locality error, which we call the certified radius , is nondecreasing as the effective noise level increases.

sections.heading: Fig. 2 (a) Local context need not be spatially contiguous.
sections.text: The first panel shows the radius-3 local contexts of the two selected patches, containing 12 and 50 nodes, respectively, including the targets. Because these sets are defined by graph distance, they need not be square or spatially contiguous: a patch that is distant on the image grid can still be nearby in G 0 G_{0} . Each ball is nevertheless connected in the graph. Thus, locality is relative to the dependence structure of the prior, rather than necessarily to proximity on the image grid.

sections.heading: Fig. 2 (b) The certified radius is nondecreasing over a bounded noise interval.
sections.text: The second panel compares the exact r ext r_{\mathrm{ext}} and certified radii r crt r_{\mathrm{crt}} at the absolute error tolerance ϵ = 10 − 3 \epsilon=10^{-3} . At low noise, the target patch’s own observation is accurate, so little additional context is needed. As noise increases, observations of correlated patches become more useful, and both radii are nondecreasing over the specified interval in this realization. r crt r_{\mathrm{crt}} is conservative: its maximum over the sweep is 16 hops, compared with 4 hops for each exact radius. The dotted line marks σ abs ≈ 1.128962 \sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}\approx 1.128962 , the endpoint specified in Cor. 2 . The corollary guarantees monotonicity of the certified radius on [ 0 , σ abs ] [0,\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}] ; the exact-radius behavior is an empirical observation in this example. Beyond this interval, the radii eventually decrease as the observations provide progressively less information about the clean signal. Indeed, J σ ∼ σ − 2 ​ Q − 1 J_{\sigma}\sim\sigma^{-2}Q^{-1} as σ → ∞ \sigma\to\infty , so both the global and local posterior means approach the zero prior mean and their absolute difference shrinks. Note that this does not mean that reconstruction improves: locality error measures the discrepancy between the two denoisers, not their error relative to the clean image.

sections.heading: Fig. 2 (c) Relative sensitivity reveals how the denoiser distributes influence across patches.
sections.text: The third panel shows that the sensitivity radius r sns r_{\mathrm{sns}} can remain broad even when the absolute locality error becomes small. As noise increases from low levels, a larger graph neighborhood is needed to capture the same fraction of the total derivative energy, consistent with the initial growth of r ext r_{\mathrm{ext}} and r crt r_{\mathrm{crt}} . At extreme noise, however, the absolute response to every observation weakens, while its relative contribution approaches a constant: ( J σ ) m ​ l 2 ∑ j ( J σ ) m ​ j 2 ⟶ ( ( Q − 1 ) m ​ l ) 2 ∑ j ( ( Q − 1 ) m ​ j ) 2 as ​ σ → ∞ . \displaystyle\frac{(J_{\sigma})_{ml}^{2}}{\sum_{j}(J_{\sigma})_{mj}^{2}}\longrightarrow\frac{((Q^{-1})_{ml})^{2}}{\sum_{j}((Q^{-1})_{mj})^{2}}\qquad\text{as }\sigma\to\infty. (39) At extreme noise, the posterior covariance approaches the prior covariance Q − 1 Q^{-1} , while the factor σ − 2 \sigma^{-2} in the Jacobian makes its absolute entries vanish. This common scale cancels under normalization, leaving a pattern determined by the prior’s covariances, which can extend to distant patches. These results show why a broad sensitivity radius can coexist with a small absolute locality error: the radius describes the distribution of influence, while the error also depends on its absolute strength. Note that in this synthetic setting, we do not claim that the sensitivity radius must increase monotonically with noise, or that observations outside the corresponding neighborhood can be removed without affecting denoising accuracy. This interpretation provides a link to denoisers trained on real-image datasets: their input–output Jacobians also describe responses to infinitesimal perturbations, so the sensitivity radius r sns r_{\mathrm{sns}} can be defined in the same way to characterize local functional context even when the population prior and exact local conditional means are unknown. Furthermore, due to ( 38 ), to the extent that learned denoisers approximate the population denoisers, their Jacobian-based sensitivity provides a measure of statistical dependence relevant to denoising.

This also follows the use of input-gradient sensitivity to study denoiser locality in Niedoba et al. (2025, Sec. 3.1) . Instead, we describe local context in terms of spatial distance and patch count. Specifically, we use the Chebyshev grid distance, a patch hop, defined as d grid ​ ( m , l ) = max ⁡ { | i m − i l | , | j m − j l | } d_{\mathrm{grid}}(m,l)=\max\{|i_{m}-i_{l}|,|j_{m}-j_{l}|\} , where i m , j m i_{m},j_{m} denote the row and column indices of patch m m , and define B r ​ ( m ) = { l : d grid ​ ( m , l ) ≤ r } B_{r}(m)=\{l:d_{\mathrm{grid}}(m,l)\leq r\} . These neighborhoods are square regions clipped to the image boundary, with radius measured in patch hops. Using the normalized derivative energy in ( 41 ), we define the sensitivity radius by r sns ​ ( m , t , q ) \displaystyle r_{\mathrm{sns}}(m,t;q) : = min ⁡ { r ∈ ℤ ≥ 0 : ∑ l ∈ B r ​ ( m ) w m ​ l ​ ( t ) ≥ q } . \displaystyle:=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{l\in B_{r}(m)}w_{ml}(t)\geq q\right\}. (42) The radius is the smallest centered Chebyshev ball containing at least a fraction q q of the normalized derivative energy. This ball measures the spatial extent of the context, but the functionally relevant local context set need not be ball-shaped. To allow arbitrary shapes, we also define a context set containing the fewest patches that together account for at least a fraction q q of the normalized derivative energy and the sensitivity count as ℬ m , t ​ ( q ) ∈ arg ​ min B ⊆ [ M ] ⁡ { | B | : ∑ l ∈ B w m ​ l ​ ( t ) ≥ q } , K q ​ ( m , t ) := | ℬ m , t ​ ( q ) | . \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m,t}(q)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{B\subseteq[M]}\left\{|B|:\sum_{l\in B}w_{ml}(t)\geq q\right\},\qquad K_{q}(m,t):=|\mathcal{B}_{m,t}(q)|. (43) We construct this set by adding patches in descending order of w m ​ l ​ ( t ) w_{ml}(t) until their cumulative energy reaches q q , breaking ties by patch index. The selected patches may be scattered or disconnected; the target patch is eligible for selection. For the population curves, we compute each target’s radius and count from the image-averaged energy in ( 41 ), then average these quantities over all 256 target patches. For the displayed sensitivity heatmaps, we apply the same construction to the normalized derivative energy of the individual noisy image. Together, these quantities distinguish spatially broad context from sparse influence carried by a few distant patches. The posterior-covariance identity ( 38 ) connects these measurements to statistical dependence remaining after observing the noisy image. Under the Jacobian approximation described above, these sensitivity-based contexts estimate the patches carrying most of the expected squared posterior cross-covariance with the target. They thus characterize the dataset’s denoising-relevant dependence through a learned predictor.

sections.heading: Estimated dependence fields resemble the exponentially local GMRF setting.
sections.text: Figure 3 reveals a pattern of denoising-relevant statistical dependence similar to that of the synthetic GMRF prior. Sensitivity is concentrated at lower noise, while its radius generally increases as noise grows, echoing the broadening of relative sensitivity in Fig. 2 . Through the posterior-covariance interpretation in ( 38 ), this suggests that predicting a patch relies on a broader set of statistical dependencies when the observation is noisier. Figures 7 and 8 corroborate this overall broadening across additional datasets and at both 90% and 95% coverage curves. The analytic GMRF setting thus provides a useful model for interpreting the estimated dependence fields of real-image datasets, beyond its role as a tractable synthetic example. Figure 7: Sensitivity and attention radii and patch counts on four datasets. Solid/dashed curves show 90%/95% coverage, computed from population maps over 1,024 held-out images and averaged over all 256 target patches.

sections.heading: The context set need not be spatially contiguous.
sections.text: The estimated dependence fields in the heatmaps show that patches carrying most of the sensitivity can form irregular or disconnected regions rather than a centered square. At lower noise, influence is concentrated near the target and selected nearby structures; at higher noise, the displayed context sets spread over a larger part of the image. The radius and patch count therefore describe complementary aspects of context: its spatial extent and the number of patches carrying a specified fraction of influence. Colors are logarithmic; gold/white contours mark 50%/95% coverage, ticks point inward, and cyan dots mark target patches.

sections.heading: Attention exhibits a related pattern of context formation.
sections.text: Head- and layer-averaged attention also tends to spread over a broader region at higher noise, although its mass is already more diffuse than sensitivity at low noise. Attention weights and input–output Jacobians are different quantities: the former are softmax-normalized logits between intermediate tokens, whereas the latter measure how the final denoised prediction responds to the original input. There is therefore no requirement that their spatial patterns agree. Their observed agreement in overall broadening is consistent with attention adapting its aggregation to the dataset’s denoising-relevant dependence structure and contributing to the formation of noise-dependent local context, as suggested by the aggregator interpretation in Sec. 4.1 and Appendix D.5 . The additional radius/count curves and heatmaps in Figs. 7 and 8 support this interpretation. Note that the comparison concerns a shared qualitative trend rather than equality of context sets: 95% attention mass and 95% squared derivative energy describe different distributions.

sections.heading: E.3.1 Motivation
sections.text: Our aggregator–predictor framework decomposes the local conditional mean into a local aggregator and a patch predictor (Def. 2 ). Sections 4.1 and 4.2 associate these operations with attention and the DiT MLP, respectively. This interpretation motivates replacing the MLP with more interpretable predictors based on retrieval from a reusable bank of learned representations, as introduced in Sec. 4.2 , with the aim of attaining comparable denoising and generative performance at a similar trainable-parameter budget. If the proposed alternatives were to fail to do so, this would indicate that their representation or training omits useful properties of an ordinary MLP for denoising. Conversely, a successful replacement provides evidence that the framework supports a useful, explicitly structured alternative. Additionally, this comparison lets us examine the effects of three design choices on empirical performance: patch-specific versus patch-shared storage, softmax cross-attention versus unnormalized GELU retrieval, and a base memory shared across layers versus independent layerwise memory. We take a baseline DiT and replace only its patch predictor with an alternative predictor, leaving everything else fixed; the following section provides the details.

sections.heading: LPLD computation and noise groups.
sections.text: LPLD’s key path applies spatial attention to each of the R R full memory grids at every layer and noise level. This is substantially more expensive than projecting a patch-shared prototype bank: distinct sampled times require distinct conditioned memory computations. We therefore draw four independent times per global batch and share each time among eight images, retaining independent Gaussian noise for each image. This allows the memory-key computation to be reused within a time group, while leaving per-image marginal objective in Eq. ( 30 ) unchanged. During training, the original H = 8 , d h ′ = 256 H=8,d_{h}^{\prime}=256 LPLD run developed severe generation artifacts and degraded denoising during training. We exclude that run from the displayed comparisons and use a separate recovery that resumes its epoch-225 checkpoint, including optimizer and EMA state, at learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} . The recovery reaches cumulative epoch 400 after 175 additional epochs and has FID 29.197 at that endpoint. Only completed post-restart measurements are drawn for its trajectory; they are not spliced onto the original curve.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: All measurements use EMA weights and the same 19,962 held-out test images. At each noise level we use t = 1 / ( 1 + σ ) t=1/(1+\sigma) to map the normalized observation to the model’s input convention. Generation uses 50 uniform time intervals from noise to data, with Heun updates and an Euler update on the last interval, and the same denominator floor of 0.05. sections.heading: (1) Different patches can retrieve from a shared patch memory.
sections.text: The patch-shared SCA and SMLP banks are more competitive than LPLD’s position-specific image-shaped memory in the corresponding parameter-budget groups. At the largest budget with H = 8 H=8 , LPLD has denoising AUC 0.013087 and FID 19.848, compared with 0.012873 and 17.145 for SCA, and 0.012777 and 15.767 for SMLP. Thus, allocating a separate stored value vector to every patch position is not necessary for competitive denoising in this setting. Sharing prototypes across positions permits a much larger bank—1,024 entries rather than 32—at a similar total parameter count. Overall, the weaker LPLD results show that the most literal learned-image retrieval construction is not automatically the easiest or most effective mechanism for patch predictor.

sections.heading: (2) GELU retrieval is more effective here than softmax retrieval.
sections.text: At every tested ( H , d h ′ ) (H,d_{h}^{\prime}) pair, SMLP has lower held-out velocity loss, denoising AUC, and FID than SCA. For example, at H = 8 , d h ′ = 512 H=8,d_{h}^{\prime}=512 , SCA and SMLP have FIDs 18.413 and 16.652, respectively, with denoising AUCs 0.012882 and 0.012716. Although SCA already includes the positive, query-dependent headwise gain η ℓ , h , t ​ ( s ) \eta_{\ell,h,t}(s) specified in Appendix D.4 , its within-head softmax coefficients remain nonnegative and coupled by normalization. In contrast, GELU allows unnormalized, potentially signed coefficients, providing a more flexible way to combine the shared values. The observed advantage is consistent with this flexibility being useful during training.

sections.heading: (3) Multiple predictor heads are usually beneficial.
sections.text: Holding the stored width fixed, H = 8 H=8 improves both held-out denoising measures over H = 1 H=1 at every tested width in all three shared-memory families. For SCA and SMLP, it also improves FID at every width. For example, at d h ′ = 1024 d_{h}^{\prime}=1024 , increasing H H from one to eight reduces FID from 22.508 to 17.145 for SCA and from 19.556 to 15.767 for SMLP. LPLD FID improves from 29.269 to 27.167 at d h ′ = 128 d_{h}^{\prime}=128 and from 24.976 to 19.848 at d h ′ = 512 d_{h}^{\prime}=512 . This suggests that multiple projections of the shared bank can be useful while keeping the total projected width fixed.

sections.heading: (4) The base memory can be shared across layers.
sections.text: The central comparison is between SMLP, whose base key–value bank is reused at every layer, and the ordinary MLP, whose vectors are independently stored in each layer. For H = 8 H=8 SMLP at d h ′ ∈ { 256,512 , 1024 } d_{h}^{\prime}\in\{256,512,1024\} , epoch-400 FIDs are 15.017, 16.652, and 15.767, compared with 19.550, 17.574, and 16.060 for the respective MLP controls. At the smallest budget, their denoising AUCs are 0.0127499 and 0.0127496, and their velocity losses are 0.076336 and 0.076360. At the middle and largest budgets, SMLP has approximately 0.24% and 1.33% higher denoising AUC, respectively, despite its lower FID. Thus the shared-memory predictor is competitive in both denoising and generation, with a small denoising tradeoff at the larger budgets. We emphasize that the result is a constructive demonstration that independently stored memory at every layer is not required for this level of performance.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: We close by noting the scope of this experiment. It is a controlled study of unconditional face generation at 64 × 64 64\times 64 resolution, with modest model sizes and one training seed per configuration. These limits constrain how broadly the findings of our experiment can be applied. We therefore do not claim that all DiT MLPs should share memory. Instead, the results support considering an explicit shared memory architecture when a common representation bank would be useful for inspection or future intervention. Our experiment shows that this architecture is feasible at least in the setting studied here.

sections.heading: Motivation and design.
sections.text: The aggregator–predictor framework separates forming a patch’s local context from predicting its clean value using learned representations. Section 4.1 associates the first operation with attention and Sec. 4.2 associates the second with the MLP. Experiment 1 finds that DiT sensitivity and attention maps exhibit related noise-dependent broadening on real images; Experiment 2 shows that explicit retrieval from a shared memory supports competitive denoising and generation quality in a controlled CelebA64 study. We now ask whether component compatibility across image domains is consistent with the proposed attention and MLP roles. This question also matters when target data or adaptation compute are limited: fine-tuning methods must decide which pretrained parameters to update, and the best choice can depend on the source and target distributions ( Kumari et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ) . The attention decomposition in ( 7 ) gives a more specific hypothesis. Within an isolated branch, QK controls spatial weights and VO transforms and transports features; the MLP admits a key–value representation for tokenwise updates. This motivates the hypothesis that source QK may remain compatible with adapted VO and MLP parameters when source and target have similar spatial context, with larger shifts associated with reduced compatibility. Source-QK compatibility may also be directional: a broadly trained source may support contextual relations needed by a narrower target, whereas the reverse transfer need not hold. We probe these hypotheses by adapting QK, VO, and MLP jointly to each target, then replacing one or more adapted groups with their source weights without further optimization. The eight resulting hybrids show how much each subset of jointly learned changes matters for reproducing the jointly adapted model.

sections.heading: Training and endpoint selection.
sections.text: We use the 20M-class DiT of Appendix E.2 on 64 × 64 64\times 64 RGB images: L = 10 L=10 , d h = 320 d_{h}=320 , H ~ = 10 \tilde{H}=10 , and MLP hidden width 1280. The twelve directions are CelebA → \to AAHQ/FFHQ/AFHQ-v2/STL-10, STL-10 → \to AAHQ/FFHQ/AFHQ-v2/CelebA, and ImageNet64 → \to AAHQ/FFHQ/AFHQ-v2/CelebA. Source training uses seed 0; adaptation starts from EMA checkpoints at source epochs 400, 800, and 800, respectively, and is repeated with two adaptation seeds. Only the attention QK and VO projections along with MLP block weights are updated jointly. Patch, position, and time embeddings, AdaLN, the output head, and other parameters stay fixed. Freezing AdaLN keeps its learned time conditioning while holding the denoising schedule constant; it assumes that this aspect of time dependence transfers across datasets. Training uses the common VP objective, global batch 32, AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , and a fresh optimizer for adaptation. For each direction, we select the checkpoint minimizing the joint model’s two-seed mean FID-50k on the monitored target split, with earlier epochs breaking ties, and use that same reference epoch for both seeds (Table 4 ). Each eight-state hybrid cube uses the selected checkpoints, EMA weights, and the same 1,024 Gaussian initial latents per state, sampled in FP32 with 50-step VP Heun. Note that since the three architectural components are adapted jointly, these eight-state swaps measure compatibility among jointly adapted components; they do not measure what independently fine-tuned restricted models could learn.

An Aggregator–Predictor View of Attention and MLPs Gyeonghun Kang Affiliation: [ Email: gk149@duke.edu William Xingxu Chen Affiliation: [ Email: wc187@duke.edu Xiang Cheng Affiliation: [ Email: xiang.cheng@duke.edu October 21, 2026 Abstract How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize? We develop an aggregator–predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers , in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs. We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius. We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation. Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key–value representation for tokenwise patch prediction. Our experiments support this view. DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern. In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance. Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction. Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention. In the middle columns, attention QK/VO and MLP weights of the source checkpoint are replaced with the corresponding fine-tuned weights; e.g., (001) means only MLP is replaced, while QK/VO are retained. For face-to-face fine-tuning, replacing only QK generates source-like faces, while replacing MLP brings visual changes: cartoon faces, bald heads, or dogs. Among the tested CelebA → \to STL-10 hybrids, coherent target-like structure appears primarily in the joint endpoint (111); reverting VO (101) leaves fragmented texture. See Sec. 5.3 and Appendix E.4 . 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow-matching models are widely used for image generation ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) becoming a standard backbone ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Li and He, 2026 ) . Growing evidence connects their generalization to representations of images and rules for reusing them . Diffusion features encode semantic and geometric information ( Baranchuk et al., 2022 ; Tang et al., 2023 ) , and aligning them with pretrained representations improves training ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Models also generate combinations absent from the training data, as shown by analyses of synthetic hierarchical data ( Okawa et al., 2023 ; Favero et al., 2025 ) . How components of DiTs realize these capabilities remains unclear. Existing explanations connect diffusion-model generalization to geometry-adaptive harmonic or balanced representations ( Kadkhodaie et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and inductive biases toward spatial locality and translation equivariance ( Kamb and Ganguli, 2025 ; Niedoba et al., 2025 ) . These accounts leave open how DiT components divide the denoising computation. Rosu et al. (2025) show that attention can implement exact score-based denoising, but they consider whole-image tokens, leaving interactions among spatial patches unresolved. An et al. (2025) associate DiT generalization with attention mimicking CNN-like spatial locality, but attention can also select input-dependent, spatially non-contiguous context (Sec. 5.1 ). We ask: How do attention, MLPs, and adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) divide the work of representing image content and learning context-dependent rules for generalization? Understanding these component roles matters for intervention: domain adaptation, concept editing, and controlled generation require deciding which computations to modify and which to preserve. In language models, interpreting MLPs as key–value memories has motivated methods for editing stored associations ( Geva et al., 2021 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ) , with related analyses in multimodal transformers ( Pan et al., 2024a ; Basu et al., 2024a ) . A functional account of DiTs could similarly guide component-wise adaptation across domains and interventions that change image content while preserving desired spatial relationships. Related work is reviewed in Appendix A . We address this question by proposing an aggregator–predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers , supported by a statistical foundation and a set of architectural and empirical observations: (1) A statistical foundation for local denoising. We justify local denoiser, in which each patch is denoised using only a subset of context patches, by identifying its statistical target and establishing when it approximates the global Bayes denoiser. Specifically, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) image priors, the global denoiser can be approximated by a radius- r r local denoiser with error decaying exponentially in r r (Thm. 1 ). We further connect existing patchwise retrieval-based explanations of generalization to this target by showing that, with sufficiently informative aggregation, a patchwise linear denoiser exactly recovers the empirical local denoiser (Thm. 3 ). (2) An aggregator–predictor interpretation of DiT components. We decompose the local denoising into context aggregation followed by patch prediction (Def. 2 ). Under this view, the algebraic structure of AdaLN-modulated attention implements an input- and noise-dependent aggregation rule: QK parameterizes spatial compatibility weights, while VO transforms the corresponding features (Sec. 4.1 ). In turn, MLP admits a key–value memory interpretation and operates on the resulting contextualized token (Sec. 4.2 ). These algebraic correspondences are exact for the isolated branches considered in Sec. 4 ; in a multilayer residual stack, the proposed roles interact and need not remain functionally separable (Appendix D.5 ). This view extends existing fixed spatial-locality accounts by allowing the relevant context to depend on the image and noise level and to include spatially non-contiguous patches. It further suggests the possibility of replacing DiT MLPs with more interpretable memory-based components, as supported by our experiments (Sec. 5.2 ). (3) Empirical evidence consistent with the proposed component roles. Across real-image datasets, DiT sensitivity fields exhibit noise-dependent context broadening resembling the GMRF setting, while attention mass shows a related qualitative trend (Sec. 5.1 ). We further construct explicit shared-memory patch predictors that retain competitive denoising and generation performance in a controlled CelebA64 study (Sec. 5.2 ). Finally, cross-domain component transplantation reveals systematic component-compatibility patterns associated with source–target spatial similarity. These patterns are consistent with, but do not uniquely identify, the proposed roles in context aggregation and patch prediction (Sec. 5.3 ). 2 Background and Problem Setup Let X 0 = ( X 0 , 1 , … , X 0 , M ) ∈ ℝ M ​ d p X_{0}=(X_{0,1},\ldots,X_{0,M})\in\mathbb{R}^{Md_{p}} be a clean image with M M patches, where X 0 , m ∈ ℝ d p X_{0,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{p}} is patch m m .
